stories.take:
Daily Faceoff reports that Brady Tkachuk spoke to media ahead of his return to Ottawa on Wednesday, saying there were "professional, personal reasons why I wasn't going to re-sign here."

The numbers say the move has gone well so far this season. Tkachuk has 6 goals and 4 assists in 9 games for FLA, in 17.04 minutes a night. Expected goals, which measure the quality of the chances a player takes, put his total at 4.65, so he is scoring about 1.35 goals above what those chances would normally produce. That is a small sample, and some of it will likely cool. The underlying play is sturdier: FLA controls 61 percent of the expected goals at five-on-five when he is on the ice, and the team's share is 7.11 percentage points better with him out there than without him. His model rate of 1.55 expected goals per 60 minutes is a real, repeatable level of chance creation. Compared with last season in OTT (22 goals and 59 points in 60 games), he is producing at a high clip, and the process behind it holds up even if the finishing eases off.

items.title: Rookie Cole Knuble scores first two goals for Flyers

stories.take:
ESPN reports that rookie forward Cole Knuble scored twice to lift the Philadelphia Flyers over the Buffalo Sabres 3-1 on Wednesday night. Per the outlet, they were the first two goals of his NHL career.

The numbers say to be careful with that line so far this season. Knuble has played only two games, and the two goals come from chances worth about 0.86 expected goals (a measure of shot quality), so he has scored 1.14 more than the model expected. His 12.07 minutes a game and his 0.7 expected goals per 60 minutes describe a depth role, not a scorer. The better sign is that PHI controls more of the play with him on the ice: its share of expected goals runs 18.45 percentage points higher with him out there, and his own five-on-five share is 54.89%.

That matters because PHI is 3-6-3 and takes only 40.7% of the expected goals overall, 37% at five-on-five. A goalie who has saved 6.8 goals above expected is keeping the team afloat. If Knuble keeps tilting the ice, he helps, but the finishing will cool.

items.title: Senators’ Linus Ullmark leaves game against Panthers
items.desc: Ullmark appeared to have tweaked something while making a save against Florida on Wednesday night.

stories.take:
Daily Faceoff reports that Senators goalie Linus Ullmark left Wednesday's game against the Panthers after appearing to tweak something while making a save against Florida. The outlet's summary gives no word yet on the severity of the injury.

It matters because Ullmark has carried a lot of Ottawa's start. Goals saved above expected, which measures how many goals a goalie has stopped compared with what an average goalie would be expected to stop on the same shots, sits at 8.24 for him through 8 games so far this season, alongside a .945 save percentage. Last season he was at -13.3 over 49 games, so this is a sharp reversal, though the sample is small. His work accounts for most of the team's 2.9 goals saved above expected, and OTT's 7-3-0 record has come with a 51.2 percent share of expected goals, which is a measure of chance quality, so the team has been decent but not dominant. Without Ullmark's goaltending, that margin gets thinner. The data doesn't say who would step in or what the backup's numbers look like, so how Ottawa holds up depends on the injury's severity.

stories.take:
Daily Faceoff reports that the Hurricanes have activated Seth Jarvis off injured reserve. Carolina also called up forward Skyler Brind'Amour and sent down forward Bradley Nadeau.

Jarvis comes back to a team that hasn't needed rescuing. Carolina is 8-2-1 for 17 points through 11 games, and it has controlled play so far this season. CAR has taken 61.5% of the expected goals, a measure of the quality of chances each side creates, and 58% at five-on-five. Its special teams look solid too: the power play generates 1.01 expected goals per game, while the penalty kill allows just 0.47 per game.

The one oddity is finishing. CAR has scored 2.8 fewer goals than its chances would suggest, so the record is probably a little short of what the play deserves. A healthy Jarvis adds another scoring option to a group already creating plenty, which is the easiest way to close that gap. The data here covers the team only, so how much he moves things on his own isn't something these numbers can show yet.

stories.take:
Per Daily Faceoff, the Bruins have signed Marat Khusnutdinov to a three-year extension carrying a $3.95 million cap hit through 2030.

The early numbers so far this season back the investment as a depth play rather than a star bet. Khusnutdinov has two goals and five points in 10 games on 13.68 minutes a night, and his goals are close to what his own chances predict: his expected goals (the quality of his shots) sit at 1.69 against two actual goals, so there is little luck inflating his line. More telling is that Boston controls 54.88% of the expected goals at five-on-five with him on the ice, and the team's share is 3.43 percentage points better with him than without. That is a useful two-way signal for a middle-six forward. For fantasy owners, though, the model projects only 0.71 expected goals per 60 minutes, so this is a steady contributor, not a scoring breakout. For Boston, the bigger picture is that the 7-2-1 record outruns the underlying play: the team holds 48.8% of expected goals overall, and goaltending has saved 9.3 goals more than expected. Locking up a player who tilts the ice the right way helps, because that cushion may not last.

stories.take:
ESPN reports the Kings broke through for their first win, a 5-2 victory over the Capitals, but lost center Quinton Byfield to an upper-body injury in the first period. Daily Faceoff reports Washington goalie Logan Thompson is day-to-day with a lower-body injury after appearing to be shaken up in the same game.

Byfield's absence would sting more than his two points in seven games so far this season suggest. LAK controlled 64% of the 5-on-5 expected goals (a measure of chance quality) while he was on the ice, and the team's share of chances rises by about 20 percentage points with him in the lineup. His own expected goals total is 1.87 against one actual goal, so a scoring bounce looked likely. Thompson's value is just as clear. He has saved 4.51 goals more than an average goalie would have against the same shots so far this season, after 28.16 over 58 games last year. WSH has otherwise been middling at 51% of 5-on-5 expected goals.

If Byfield misses time, going by how the coach has used his players, Scott Laughton (14:43 a night) is next in line for his minutes. Corey Perry, the busiest man on the second power-play unit, is the likeliest to move up to the first.

stories.take:
The Hockey News reports that Penguins GM Kyle Dubas is at a crossroads after a slow start: he can chase one last playoff spot or begin selling pieces of an aging roster for the future, and the outlet argues selling is the right move.

The numbers suggest Pittsburgh's record is worse than its play. The Penguins are 3-5-1 with 7 points through 9 games, but they hold 49.3% of the expected goals (a measure of chance quality, so roughly an even split with opponents). At 5-on-5 that climbs to 55%, a clear edge. Pittsburgh has also scored 3 fewer goals than its chances would predict so far this season, which points to finishing and bad puck luck more than a broken team. Goaltending sits right at expectation, with goals saved above expected at 0, so the goalie isn't the culprit either.

That matters because a nine-game sample is small, and the underlying play doesn't yet make the case for a teardown. If the finishing recovers, the standings could improve without a roster change. Dubas has reason to wait before deciding which way to go.

The early numbers say Ottawa's 6-3-0 start, good for 12 points in nine games, is a bit better than the underlying play. The Senators' share of expected goals (a measure of chance quality, where 50% is an even split) is 50.6% so far this season, and 49% at five-on-five, so they are roughly breaking even rather than dominating. The gap shows in goals minus expected, which sits at -3.8: the skaters have scored well below what their chances suggest. Goalies have covered for that, with goals saved above expected at +2.2, meaning the netminding has stopped more than the shot quality predicted. The special teams look steady, not elite: the power play generates 0.82 expected goals per game and the penalty kill allows 0.75. For Green, the extension rewards results, but the data suggests the finishing should improve, and that matters more than the record if the goaltending cools.

items.desc: The Toronto Maple Leafs got bad news when star center John Tavares suffered a major injury Thursday against Buffalo. But while the Buds will miss Tavares, other Leafs players now have a golden chance to step up and contribute meaningfully. Which Leafs will…

stories.take:
The Hockey News reports that Toronto center John Tavares suffered a major injury Thursday against Buffalo, and that the Maple Leafs' depth players now have a chance to step up in his absence.

The numbers suggest the drop-off may be smaller than his name implies. So far this season, Tavares has two goals and five assists in seven games, but his 5-on-5 share of expected goals (the quality of chances created versus allowed) is just 29.91%, meaning Toronto has been badly outchanced with him on the ice. The team's share of expected goals is 18.96 percentage points better when he is off it. That is a small sample, but it points to a player who has been a drag on play-driving even as his point total looked fine. His own expected goals of 2.49 sit about half a goal above his two actual goals, so his scoring has not been inflated by luck either.

For the Leafs overall, the concern is larger than one player. Toronto sits at 3-4-2 with a 45.7% expected goal share, and goalie play (2.2 goals saved above expected) is propping up the results. Someone has to drive the play, and so far that has not been Tavares.

stories.take:
The Athletic lists Dallas Stars defenseman Tyler Myers and Buffalo Sabres forward Josh Norris as under-the-radar trade candidates this season, part of a piece naming one candidate for every NHL team.

The numbers so far this season give neither team much urgency to move them. Myers has no points in seven games for Dallas, and the Stars generate 44.34% of the 5-on-5 expected goals with him on the ice, which is 7.54 percentage points worse than when he sits. At 14.49 minutes a night, he is a depth defender whose results are not hurting him unfairly, since his own expected goals are just 0.13. Norris is a different case. His 5-on-5 share is a break-even 50.85%, but his 1.24 own expected goals against 1 goal points to a bit of bad finishing, not a bad process, and Buffalo's 4-3-1 start looks fine underneath, at 52.1% of total expected goals. His 0.84 model expected goals per 60 and last season's 13 goals in 44 games suggest the production is there to come. Both samples are tiny, so this is a read on the early picture, not a verdict.
